title: Afternoon Tea
author: Adrian Neibauer
summary: Teacher and writer Adrian Neibauer reflects on family dinner as a sacred ritual and on how a conversation with SEMH author Kieran Smith about British tea culture led him to add a daily afternoon tea at home and to value his classroom tea station more deliberately. He describes offering herbal tea to a student who arrives gloomy or unwell, and observes that the other students read a cup on a peer's desk as comfort for someone in need, not a privilege. He sets this against American hustle culture and a classroom culture that presses to maximize every instructional minute. The essay includes a brief history of English tea and afternoon tea, interleaved with passages from Austen and Henry James. At home, a month of tea at 4:15 has lengthened conversations with his teenagers and made dinner more agreeable. He concludes that small shared rituals build community and that offering tea is a quiet act of resistance to dehumanizing pressures.
points: A small, repeatable ritual such as a tea station can change body language, relax anxious students, and build peer empathy without any explanation.
Students intuitively understand that a cup of tea is comfort for someone in need, not a reward for favorites.
Slowing down is framed as a counterweight to pressure to maximize every instructional minute.
The same practice at home, a daily 4:15 tea, restored longer conversations with teenagers.
The Kieran Smith idea of regulating before educating supports soft starts and calm-down spaces for dysregulated children.
quotes: Family dinner is one of our most sacred rituals. From the time our children were born, my wife and I insisted that, no matter the schedule, we all congregate to the kitchen table for our evening meal.
We have laughed, cried, argued, sang, and danced together. It has been (and always will be) a safe space for everyone.
American hustle culture is antagonistic to slow, communal rituals.
I have noticed that when a student is holding a mug of tea or hot chocolate, their body language changes. Their shoulders relax and their anxiety slackens.
In reality, however, without me explaining, students intuitively understand that drinking a cup of herbal tea is not a privilege for a favorite student; it is a comfort given to someone in need.
No one argues at afternoon tea. We chitchat about our days and then spend a few quiet moments decompressing from work/school before reconvening in the kitchen for dinner.
Offering a cup of tea to a student is a small act of resistance to the constant dehumanizing pressures to maximize every instructional minute of the day.
Pouring a cup of tea reminds me that teaching and learning can, and do, happen in slow and messy ways.
